questions.question: Describe Christiaan Barnard's background and the discoveries that made heart surgery possible.
questions.expected_answer: Christiaan Barnard was born in 1922 in Beaufort West, studied medicine at the University of Cape Town and trained in heart surgery at the University of Minnesota. He set up a heart surgery unit at Groote Schuur Hospital and practised heart transplants on dogs with his team. Heart surgery depended on anaesthetics, sterile theatres, blood transfusions, X-rays and the heart-lung machine, which takes over pumping and adding oxygen to blood while the heart is stopped.

questions.question: Describe the events of the first human heart transplant in December 1967.
questions.expected_answer: Louis Washkansky, a fifty-three-year-old shop owner with a failing heart and diabetes, agreed to a transplant. On the second of December 1967, Denise Darvall, aged twenty-five, suffered fatal brain injuries in a car accident, and her father agreed to donate her heart. That night, Barnard and a team of about thirty placed her heart in Washkansky's chest at Groote Schuur, and an electric shock started it beating. Washkansky died of pneumonia eighteen days later, but the heart worked until the end.

questions.question: What happened to heart transplants after 1967, and what does Hamilton Naki's story show?
questions.expected_answer: Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived about nineteen months. Many surgeons tried transplants, but most patients died of rejection and infection, so numbers dropped until cyclosporine in the early nineteen-eighties controlled rejection; today thousands are done each year and many patients live ten years or more. Hamilton Naki, a black laboratory assistant denied medical training under apartheid, became highly skilled at animal surgery and trained many doctors, and was honoured with a degree in 2003, showing the injustice of apartheid.
